content.title: About
content.content: Apple pie filling is a ready‑made mixture of fresh apples, sugar, spices and sometimes lemon juice, designed for quick and convenient preparation of apple pie. Apples are sliced, combined with cinnamon, nutmeg and sweetened, then the filling is ready to use.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional American filling often mixes sweet and tart apple varieties for balanced flavor.
Cinnamon added to the filling provides antioxidant benefits and enhances aroma.
Classic recipes sometimes include a bit of butter to make the filling juicier.
Apple filling can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or frozen for up to 3 months.
There are sugar‑free versions that rely on the natural sweetness of apples and a touch of honey.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Apples contain soluble and insoluble fiber that supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C in apples helps boost the immune system and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in apples protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Heart‑friendly
items.content: Fiber and potassium help lower cholesterol levels and maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Apple pie filling contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Prepared fillings often contain added sugar, which may be unsuitable for people with diabetes or those limiting sugar intake.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to cinnamon or nutmeg, causing allergic reactions.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The natural acidity of apples can irritate a sensitive stomach in some people.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Commercial versions may contain preservatives that are not preferred by all consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the filling as the base for apple pie, stir into muffins, pastries, pancakes, or serve warm as a dessert with ice cream. It can also be mixed with cottage cheese or yogurt for a healthy snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags – up to 3 months. Thaw in the fridge or at room temperature before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Biryani with chicken is a fragrant Indian dish made from long‑grain basmati rice, marinated chicken, spices (coriander, cumin, turmeric, garam masala) and vegetables. It is traditionally layered so that the rice absorbs the juices of the meat and spices, creating a rich flavor and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word biryani comes from the Persian “birinj”, meaning “fried rice”.
There are many regional variations: South Indian versions often use coconut milk, while North Indian ones use yogurt.
Traditionally the dish is cooked in a heavy clay pot (dolsah) with a tight seal to trap steam.
Chicken is commonly marinated in yogurt and lemon juice, which tenderizes the meat.
Biryani is usually served with raita (yogurt sauce) and a fresh vegetable salad.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Basmati rice supplies slowly digestible carbohydrates that help maintain steady energy levels.

items.title: Contains beneficial spices
items.content: Turmeric, cumin and coriander have anti‑inflammatory and antioxidant properties.

items.title: B vitamins
items.content: Biryani delivers vitamins B6 and B12, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Yogurt in the marinade and the spices promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to coriander, cumin or turmeric.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Biryani is often seasoned with salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken can harbor salmonella; ensure the meat is fully cooked.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish can be calorie‑rich due to oil and nuts, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve biryani hot, typically with raita, pickled vegetables (achar) and naan bread. Garnish with fresh cilantro or mint for extra brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. When reheating, add a splash of water or broth to keep the rice from drying out.

chicken-drumstick-baked-or-broiled-skin-.title: Chicken drumstick, baked or broiled, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: A chicken drumstick prepared by baking or broiling is a common item in fast‑food restaurants and casual dining. The skin stays on, providing flavor, moisture and a crispy texture. It is usually served hot, often with sauces or side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks contain more fat than breast meat, making them juicier and more flavorful.
When baked, the skin forms a golden crust that locks in moisture.
In the United States the term "drumsticks" is widely used for this cut, especially in kids' meals.
Asian cuisines often marinate drumsticks in soy sauce, honey and spices before grilling.
Drumsticks are a staple of barbecue menus, glazed with sweet‑tangy sauces and cooked low and slow.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken drumsticks provide high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from meat helps maintain hemoglobin levels and prevents anemia.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Collagen in the skin
items.content: The skin contains collagen, which may benefit skin and joint health.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Drumsticks are fattier than breast meat, so they should be limited in low‑fat diets.

items.title: Sodium in prepared dishes
items.content: Fast‑food versions often come with salty sauces that can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked drumsticks may harbor salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 165 °F (74 °C).

items.title: Chicken protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken meat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drumsticks are typically eaten hot, pulling the meat off the bone. The crispy skin can be eaten as is or dipped in sauces. They pair well with fries, salads, or barbecue sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh drumsticks keep in the refrigerator at 2–4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen, they last up to 6 months at –18 °C. Thaw frozen pieces in the fridge before cooking, and store cooked drumsticks in an airtight container for no more than 3 days.

chicken-or-turkey-salad-made-with-mayonn.title: Chicken or Turkey Salad with Mayonnaise

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey salad with mayonnaise is a ready‑to‑eat dish where boiled or roasted poultry is diced and mixed with vegetables (commonly cucumber, tomato, onion) and a creamy mayonnaise dressing. It is usually served cold as a light meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mayonnaise‑based salads became popular in the USSR during the 1950s as a quick cafeteria dish.
Chicken and turkey provide high‑quality protein, and the mayonnaise adds richness and satiety.
Traditional recipes use boiled chicken breast, but many prefer roasted turkey for a deeper flavor.
Classic Soviet mayonnaise was made from eggs, vegetable oil, and mustard; today most people use store‑bought versions.
The salad is often garnished with fresh herbs, hard‑boiled eggs, or olives.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Poultry meat supplies complete protein needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken and turkey are high in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Poultry provides heme iron, aiding oxygen transport in the body.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Mayonnaise adds calories from fat, making the salad a good energy source when eaten in moderation.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Mayonnaise is rich in saturated fats and calories, so portion control is important for weight‑watchers.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Traditional mayonnaise contains eggs, which can trigger reactions in allergic individuals.

items.title: Bacterial growth risk
items.content: If left at room temperature for more than 2 hours, the salad can become a breeding ground for harmful bacteria.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Store‑bought mayonnaise often contains added salt; people with hypertension should monitor total sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a standalone dish, a side, or a topping for sandwiches, wraps, and rolls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator and consume within 3‑4 days. Above 4 °C it can spoil quickly.

content.title: About
content.content: The sugar‑free energy drink is a zero‑calorie refresher containing caffeine, taurine, B‑vitamins and natural flavorings. It is designed to boost alertness and concentration without added sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink provides about 80 mg of caffeine per 250 ml, comparable to a regular cup of coffee.
Being sugar‑free, it fits low‑glycemic diets.
B‑vitamins help support cellular energy metabolism.
Taurine may aid physical endurance during intense exercise.
Artificial sweeteners give a sweet taste without calories.

items.title: Increased alertness
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving focus and reaction time.

items.title: Supports energy metabolism
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, B3, B6 and B12 assist in converting food into usable energy.

items.title: Enhanced endurance
items.content: Taurine may help muscles use oxygen more efficiently.

items.title: No added sugar
items.content: Suitable for individuals monitoring blood glucose levels.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The water content helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some people may experience anxiety, insomnia or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine can amplify the effects of stimulants and reduce the efficacy of sedatives.

items.title: Excessive intake
items.content: Frequent consumption may lead to elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: They can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in certain individuals.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Consume the drink chilled, preferably in the first half of the day. Avoid mixing with alcohol and limit intake to 2–3 servings per day.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 7 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Flavored rice, brown and wild is a blend of whole‑grain brown rice and wild rice grains seasoned with natural herbs and spices. It offers a rich nutty flavor, subtle aromatic notes, and a firm texture while retaining the nutritional benefits of whole grains.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The combination of brown and wild rice provides a more complex flavor and texture than plain white rice.
Wild rice is not a true rice but the seed of several aquatic grasses native to North America.
Brown rice retains the bran and germ, making it more nutritious than polished white rice.
Seasonings typically include dried garlic, onion, paprika, and herbs such as thyme or rosemary, without artificial additives.
The blend is popular in low‑glycemic diets because of its slower impact on blood sugar.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Both brown and wild rice supply dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of magnesium and selenium
items.content: These minerals aid muscle function, nerve health, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Helps maintain stable blood glucose levels, beneficial for pre‑diabetic individuals.

items.title: Contains plant protein
items.content: Provides about 7 g of protein per 100 g, contributing to satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients in brown and wild rice help combat free radicals.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to rice.

items.title: Arsenic content
items.content: Brown rice can accumulate trace amounts of arsenic; varied grain consumption is advised.

items.title: Digestive sensitivity
items.content: High fiber may cause gas or bloating in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Flavored rice, brown and wild can be cooked as a side dish, added to salads, soups, bowls, or casseroles. Rinse the rice, then simmer 1 part rice to 2 parts water for 20‑25 minutes until tender but still slightly firm.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For storage longer than six months, keep in the refrigerator to prevent mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Flaxseed oil is obtained from the seeds of the flax plant (Linum usitatissimum) by cold pressing. It has a light yellow color, a characteristic nutty aroma, and is one of the richest plant sources of alpha‑linolenic acid (omega‑3).

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Flax has been cultivated for more than 6,000 years and was used in ancient Egypt for lamps and cosmetics.
Flaxseed oil contains about 55 % polyunsaturated fats, of which over 50 % is alpha‑linolenic acid.
When stored in a cool dark place, the oil can retain its quality for up to 12 months, but it oxidizes quickly when exposed to heat.
In vegan cooking, 1 tbsp oil + 3 tbsp water can replace one egg in baking.
Traditional medicine has used flaxseed oil to improve skin and hair health.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Alpha‑linolenic acid supports cardiovascular health by lowering triglycerides and reducing inflammation.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber and mucilage in the oil help regular bowel movements and protect the intestinal lining.

items.title: Skin health
items.content: Omega‑3 and vitamin E moisturize the skin and reduce dryness and irritation.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lignans and vitamin E neutralize free radicals, slowing cellular aging.

items.title: Hormonal balance
items.content: Polyunsaturated fatty acids are precursors for prostaglandins, influencing hormonal functions.

items.title: Oxidation risk
items.content: When heated above 120 °C, the oil rapidly loses its beneficial properties and forms harmful compounds.

items.title: Flax allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to flax seeds or the oil.

items.title: Interaction with blood thinners
items.content: High doses of omega‑3 can enhance the effect of anticoagulant medications.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although nutrient‑dense, the oil provides about 900 kcal per 100 ml, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use flaxseed oil in cold dishes: salad dressings, smoothies, yogurt, oatmeal. It is not recommended for frying; choose an oil with a higher smoke point for high‑heat cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the oil in a dark glass bottle in the refrigerator. Properly stored, it stays fresh for 6‑12 months. Discard if it develops a bitter smell or becomes cloudy.

content.title: About
content.content: Goat cheese is made from goat's milk and has a slightly tangy, mildly sharp flavor. It is softer and more crumbly than most cow‑milk cheeses and is commonly used in salads, baked dishes, or enjoyed on its own as a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Goat's milk contains less lactose than cow's milk, making goat cheese easier to digest for some people with mild lactose intolerance.
Traditional goat cheese production originates from the Mediterranean region, where goats are a primary source of milk.
Goat cheese typically provides more calcium per serving than many cow‑milk cheeses.
It can be produced fresh or aged; aged varieties develop a stronger aroma and firmer texture.
In several cultures goat cheese is considered a delicacy and is served with honey, nuts, or fruit.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Calcium supports bone and teeth health and plays a role in muscle contraction and nerve signaling.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for red blood cell formation and neurological function.

items.title: Lower lactose content
items.content: The reduced lactose makes goat cheese a better option for those with mild lactose sensitivity.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Protein aids tissue growth and repair and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Goat cheese contains monounsaturated fatty acids that are beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: People allergic to milk proteins or casein may react to goat cheese.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Some goat cheeses are heavily salted, which can be problematic for individuals with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Although lower than many cow‑milk cheeses, goat cheese still contains saturated fats and should be consumed in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Goat cheese can be enjoyed fresh, crumbled over salads, mixed into pastas, pizza, casseroles, or paired with fruit, honey, and nuts. It is also used in sauces and fillings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store goat cheese in the refrigerator, wrapped in parchment paper or in an airtight container. For storage longer than a week, keep it in the coldest part of the fridge. Discard cheese that develops an off‑odor or mold that is not the natural white rind of aged varieties.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned chicken noodle soup is a ready‑to‑eat soup packed in a sealed can. It contains chicken broth, small noodles, pieces of chicken meat, and vegetables. Made according to a traditional recipe, it retains aroma and nutritional value.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canning allows the soup to be stored for 2‑3 years without refrigeration.
The broth is often enhanced with monosodium glutamate for flavor.
Noodles are usually small so they soften quickly in hot water.
Canned soups are popular for camping, office lunches, and emergency kits.
Some manufacturers add a small amount of vitamin C to preserve color.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Chicken pieces provide easily digestible animal protein important for tissue repair.

items.title: Electrolytes
items.content: The broth supplies sodium and potassium, helping maintain fluid balance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken broth is rich in B6 and B12 vitamins, supporting normal metabolism.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: Carbohydrates from the noodles give a fast source of energy, useful during physical activity.

items.title: Soothing effect
items.content: A warm broth can be comforting and may help ease mild cold symptoms.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned soups often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: To ensure long shelf life, preservatives may be added, which some people prefer to avoid.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to poultry should avoid this product.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate
items.content: Sensitive individuals may experience headaches or flushing from MSG.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Open the can, pour the contents into a pot and bring to a boil for 3‑5 minutes. Optionally garnish with fresh herbs, green onions, or a dash of hot sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 2‑3 days.
